phenomena.name: 年龄分层发病率分化
phenomena.description: 城市中不同年龄组可能因接触机会、健康状态和社会活动方式差异，呈现不同的感染发生率与增长轨迹；这种分化可能随疫情阶段和防控措施变化而改变。

phenomena.name: 环境特异性聚集持续
phenomena.description: 学校、工作场所和社区活动环境可能形成传播特征不同的感染聚集；某些环境中的聚集可能较家庭接触更短暂或更持久，并影响城市感染事件的时间分布。

phenomena.name: 家庭续发感染集中
phenomena.description: 家庭成员之间持续日常接触可能使家庭成为感染传播的集中场所；由指示病例引发的家庭内续发感染比例可能在不同家庭结构和活动模式下出现差异。

phenomena.name: 隐匿传播遮蔽
phenomena.description: 部分感染者在症状出现前、症状轻微或未被识别时仍保持社会接触，可能造成不依赖于显性症状检测的传播，使观测到的病例变化低估实际感染活动。

phenomena.name: 追踪能力饱和
phenomena.description: 当感染人数增长超过公共卫生部门识别和追踪密切接触者的能力时，追踪覆盖率和隔离及时性可能下降，进而改变后续传播链的阻断效果。

phenomena.name: 依从性异质反馈
phenomena.description: 居民对减少活动、隔离或检测建议的遵守程度存在差异；这种异质性可能削弱防控措施的实际效果，并随疫情感知和措施执行范围变化而形成反馈。

phenomena.name: 干预时机人群转移
phenomena.description: 不同时间实施或调整的学校、工作场所和社区防控措施可能将感染负担在不同年龄组或社会环境之间转移，导致疫情增长过程出现阶段性人群结构变化。

phenomena.name: 社区活动复燃
phenomena.description: 在城市整体感染活动下降后，社区活动网络中较广泛的联系可能促成局部感染再次增加，使不同区域或人群出现不同步的复燃过程。

edge.semantic_rationale: More per-agent new-exposure transitions raise the flow of exposure events that can be attributed to contact layers, so layer-level incidence per recorded edge can rise when these transitions cluster in a layer rather than being diffuse.
New household exposures increase the chance that a household-layer dyad accumulates at least one attributed exposure, lifting the fraction of dyads with any attributed event.
If new exposures concentrate in some age bands, between-band exposure hazards diverge, increasing cross-band dispersion even when total exposure activity is unchanged.

Cohorts of new exposures later enter infectious states; if they are distributed unevenly across quarantine-status groups, the silent share of infectious person-steps in those groups can shift after the exposure-to-infectious delay.
New exposures that are layer-attributed alter relative layer composition; an increase in exposures in one setting raises its share of attributed transitions.
Post-trough new exposures feed layer-attributed incidence after the trough; if they occur preferentially in a layer, that layer's after-versus-at-trough incidence ratio rises.
Source-attributed exposures are the events entering layer incidence numerators; more attributed exposures per edge raise layer incidence, especially when attribution is concentrated in a layer.
Source-attributed household exposures add dyads to the ever-attacked set, increasing the fraction of household dyads with any attributed exposure.
Attributed exposures concentrated among particular ages can widen band-specific exposure hazards, raising cross-band dispersion.
Attributed exposures seed later infectious individuals; uneven attribution across quarantine-status groups can change the silent share after progression to infectiousness.
Attributed exposures determine which layers receive incident events; a shift toward one layer raises its exposure share.
Attributed exposures after the trough drive layer-specific post-trough incidence; concentration in a layer raises its post-trough ratio relative to the trough.
More quarantined agents in a layer lower the quarantined group's mean in-layer degree relative to non-quarantined agents, reducing the layer suppression ratio through behavioural withdrawal.
Quarantine removes agents from contact layers, reducing exposure events per remaining edge, so layer incidence per edge can fall when quarantine covers active layer members.
Quarantine changes which layers remain active; settings with many quarantined members lose exposure share while less affected layers gain share.
Quarantine after the trough can suppress layer-specific resurgence; layers with higher quarantine coverage show lower post-trough incidence ratios.
Quarantining an index case in a household dyad reduces subsequent attributed household exposures, lowering the fraction of dyads with any attributed event.
Heterogeneous per-agent contact ratios under quarantine aggregate into the layer-level ratio: agents who reduce contacts more strongly lower the quarantined mean degree, increasing suppression.
Agents with lower quarantine contact ratios contribute fewer layer contacts and exposures, reducing layer incidence per edge when such adherence is common in the layer.
Adherence differences shift exposure activity from layers where quarantined agents withdraw toward layers where they remain active, changing layer exposure shares.
Higher adherence in a layer suppresses post-trough attributed incidence more than at the trough, lowering that layer's post-trough ratio.
Household dyad members with lower quarantine contact ratios sustain more in-home contact, raising the chance that the dyad accumulates an attributed exposure.
If adherence differs by age, quarantine contact reduction is uneven across age bands, widening band-specific exposure hazards and increasing dispersion.
Agents becoming ever-exposed earlier deplete the local susceptible pool, so the aggregate susceptible share remaining at the city infectious trough is lower.
Greater cumulative individual exposure leaves fewer susceptible agents available to fuel a rebound, damping the post-trough resurgence amplitude.
Accumulated ever-exposed state among agents reduces susceptible recruitment after the trough, limiting the aggregate post-trough growth rate of infectious agents.
Higher per-agent contact degree in a layer increases exposure opportunities along recorded edges, raising the layer-level exposure incidence per edge.
Agents with many contacts in a layer can sustain transmission chains across consecutive sampled steps, lengthening the layer's active exposure run.
Heterogeneous per-agent degree across layers concentrates exposure activity in high-degree settings, shifting the cross-layer entropy of attributed exposures.
When individual contact degree grows unevenly across layers, the layer composition of attributed exposures drifts away from its early-run reference.
High per-agent layer degree preserves transmission opportunities after the trough, supporting faster aggregate growth of infectious agents.
Higher individual contact degree provides more channels for renewed transmission, increasing the size of the post-trough rebound.
Agents with contacts spread across layers can seed post-trough increases in multiple settings, broadening the share of layers with resurgence.
Within-layer degree dispersion creates core-periphery contact patterns that make some layers dominate exposure production, changing cross-layer incidence entropy.
Dispersed degree within a layer leaves high-contact agents able to restart transmission after the trough, increasing post-trough infectious growth.
Strong within-layer degree inequality can produce concentrated superspreading events that amplify the post-trough rebound.
Individual household-attributed exposure events convert previously unaffected household dyads into attacked dyads, raising the fraction of dyads with any attributed exposure.
Repeated household-attributed exposures concentrate in a subset of dyads, increasing dispersion of cumulative attributed exposures across household dyads.
More household-attributed individual exposures raise the household layer's share of attributed exposures, shifting layer composition over time.
Household-attributed exposure chains can persist through low-incidence periods and reseed transmission, increasing post-trough rebound amplitude.
Silently infectious agents remain in contact and contribute infection pressure in their age bands, raising the band-level exposure hazard.
Silent infectious agents active in contact layers generate exposures along recorded edges, increasing layer exposure incidence per edge.
A larger silent infectious pool lowers the number of new diagnoses per infectious person-step, reducing observed detection coverage.
Silent infectious episodes accumulate undiagnosed ever-exposed agents, increasing the ratio of never-diagnosed to ever-diagnosed infections.
Undiagnosed silent infectious agents are less likely to be quarantined, lowering population quarantine coverage relative to observed infections.
Silent infectious agents continue normal activity, attenuating the population-wide decline in contact volume after interventions.
Ongoing silent transmission offsets the growth reduction expected around quarantine onset, weakening the observed before-after growth contrast.
Silent infections surviving the trough continue generating new infections, raising post-trough growth of the infectious population.
Hidden infectious activity provides a reservoir that can seed a larger rebound after the observed infectious minimum.
Quarantine-status groups that generate more exposures per silent infectious person-step expand the silent infectious pool, increasing silent prevalence share.
High silent exposure yield in groups after the trough sustains aggregate infectious growth by continuously adding new infections.
Groups with high silent exposure yield can drive a larger rebound because their hidden transmission chains remain active through the decline.
Higher per-edge known-contact incidence in layers brings more infections to diagnosis through tracing, raising new diagnoses per infectious person-step.
Layer-level tracing yield converts more flagged contacts into quarantined agents, increasing population quarantine coverage.
Higher known-contact incidence per layer edge increases the standing caseload of known contacts at the population level.
Stronger layer tracing yield removes contacts from transmission chains, reducing the fuel available for a post-trough rebound.
Effective per-edge tracing in some layers suppresses those settings after the trough, reducing the share of layers that show renewed incidence.
Heterogeneous individual reductions in degree under quarantine create a wider spread of contact degree among quarantined agents.
Agents whose quarantine degree remains close to normal sustain transmission after the trough, increasing aggregate infectious growth.
Heterogeneous adherence leaves some quarantined agents with high contact degree, providing channels for a larger rebound.
If later-exposed cohorts have a different age structure from early cohorts, the timing of individual first exposures shifts the aggregate age composition of incident exposures.
Cohort timing changes which age groups contribute new exposures, moving the median age of agents with exposure transitions.
Exposures occurring later in the run feed the post-trough infectious pool, increasing measured growth after the trough.
A later distribution of individual first exposures places more new infections after the trough, raising the rebound amplitude.
Drift in age-band shares of exposure transitions changes the weighting of age groups, moving the median age of new exposures.
When exposure incidence shifts toward particular age bands, cumulative attack ratios diverge further between the most and least affected bands.
Age-band exposure share drift changes the composition of new exposures relative to susceptible person-time, increasing composition mismatch.
Drift toward more active or less immune age bands can sustain new infections after the trough, raising aggregate post-trough growth.
A shift in exposure burden toward age bands with more remaining susceptible contacts can amplify the post-trough rebound.
Differential post-trough incidence across age bands widens cumulative attack ratios between the most and least affected bands.
Age-selective post-trough exposure increases alter the exposure composition relative to susceptible person-time, raising composition mismatch.
When some age bands have higher post-trough incidence ratios than others, the age composition of incident exposures shifts away from its early-run reference.
Age bands with high post-trough exposure rates contribute disproportionately to new infections, increasing aggregate post-trough infectious growth.
Age-selective post-trough increases in exposure rates add to the overall infectious pool, raising the observed resurgence amplitude.

Agents with longer cumulative silent infectious duration continue to contact others while undiagnosed, increasing the rate at which susceptible age-band members become exposed; this raises the band-level exposure hazard beyond what would occur if silent infectious periods were shorter.

Silent infectious agents sustain contact activity in their settings, so layers with such agents experience repeated exposure events across consecutive steps, lengthening the layer's consecutive active-step run.
In a household dyad, a silently infectious index case with longer duration has more opportunities to expose the partner, increasing the dyad's attributed secondary exposure count.

Being flagged as a known contact typically triggers quarantine and reduced social activity, which lowers the exposure hazard in the agent's age band by removing potential transmitters from contact networks.
Known-contact flags lead to quarantine, reducing the number of active transmitters in contact layers and thereby shortening the layer's consecutive run of exposure events.
When a household member is flagged as a known contact and quarantined, secondary exposures within that dyad are reduced, lowering the dyad's attributed secondary count.

Known-contact flags are the trigger for quarantine; the layer-specific contact degree of newly quarantined flagged agents defines the tracing workload per index, so more flagged agents in a layer increase the layer's per-index contact load.
Quarantined agents who achieve zero contacts contribute no exposures, reducing the exposure hazard in their age band compared with bands where quarantined agents maintain contacts.
Full contact suppression by quarantined agents removes exposure events from their layers, which can break the layer's consecutive active run and shorten its length.
A quarantined household member with zero contacts cannot generate secondary exposures in the dyad, lowering the dyad's attributed secondary count.

Zero-contact quarantined agents contribute zero degree to the per-index contact load; their presence in the newly quarantined set lowers the layer's average contact load because the average includes these zeros.

A longer exposure-to-diagnosis interval means the agent remains undetected and potentially infectious for more steps, increasing the number of exposure events generated among susceptible age-band members and raising the band's exposure hazard.

Longer intervals delay diagnosis and isolation, so exposed agents continue contacting others in their layers for more steps, sustaining layer-level exposure activity and lengthening consecutive active runs.
In a household dyad, a longer exposure-to-diagnosis interval for the index case provides more time for within-dyad transmission before isolation, increasing the dyad's secondary exposure count.

Higher household-layer degree for an agent increases repeated close-contact exposure within the household setting; when such agents are concentrated in particular age bands, sustained household transmission can raise those bands' cumulative attack ratios rather than merely reflecting a precomputed aggregate.

Agents carrying larger per-layer contact-weight loads are more likely to generate new exposures through their setting-specific contacts; if this load is unevenly distributed across ages, the affected age bands can accumulate higher attack ratios over the run.

An agent with more household-layer contacts participates in more dyadic pairs that can receive secondary exposure; variation in household degree therefore changes how unevenly attributed secondary events are distributed across household dyads.

Symptomatic-but-undiagnosed agents continue normal social contact without entering surveillance; if this state is more common in some age groups, those groups contribute disproportionately to new exposure transitions and shift the age-band composition of incident exposure activity.

Longer delay from known-contact flag to quarantine leaves source agents and their household contacts active for more steps; this can create additional secondary exposure events in some household dyads and increase dispersion of attributed counts across dyads.

When individual tracing delays are long and uneven, newly quarantined index agents may accumulate different numbers of active layer contacts before isolation; this uneven accumulation can widen the cross-layer dispersion of per-index contact load.

Agents with large household-layer degree retain more recorded contacts even while quarantined; heterogeneity in household degree among quarantined agents therefore contributes to wider dispersion of observed contact degree in the quarantined subgroup.

Post-trough exposure transitions in particular age bands add incident activity after the citywide infectious minimum; if resurgence is age-selective, these late exposures change the band shares of new exposure transitions at subsequent steps.

High contact-weight load within a layer makes repeated exposure between connected agents more likely; in the household-like layer this can produce additional secondary events in some dyads and increase dyad-level dispersion of attributed secondary counts.

Undiagnosed symptomatic agents remain in contact networks and can later be linked to known-contact tracing in different settings; if they are unevenly distributed across layers, the resulting per-index contact load becomes more dispersed across layers.

A higher exposure hazard in an age band raises the per-agent probability that a susceptible member of that band transitions from not exposed to exposed at the next observed step, so band-level hazard can drive individual new-exposure events.

When exposure shares are misaligned with susceptible person-time, exposure pressure is disproportionately borne by bands with more remaining susceptible person-time; this can elevate the measured hazard in those bands as susceptible depletion and exposure targeting co-evolve.

High edge-set turnover breaks contact continuity within a setting, reducing the chance that any recorded edge repeatedly carries transmission and thereby lowering attributed exposure incidence per edge in that layer.

As a larger fraction of household-layer dyads accumulates attributed exposure, household transmission becomes more saturated; an individual exposure is then more likely to be recorded in the household-attributed category rather than in other settings.

A quarantine-status group with high exposure yield per silent infectious person-step exerts greater transmission pressure on its members, raising the probability that an individual in that group shows a new exposure transition.

A longer population-average symptom-to-diagnosis interval implies diagnosis occurs later in the disease course, extending the period during which an individual can remain infectious while undiagnosed.

When more known contacts are generated per new diagnosis, each index case implies more layer-specific contact investigations, increasing the per-index contact load that must be examined within contact layers.

High dispersion of contact degree among quarantined agents implies a heavy lower tail of very low-contact behaviour; an individual quarantined agent is then more likely to fall into the fully suppressed zero-contact category.

A lower population-level quarantine suppression ratio indicates stronger overall activity reduction among quarantined agents, shaping the adherence context in which an individual quarantined agent’s own in-quarantine contact ratio is realised.

As the age composition of incident exposures drifts toward groups that were less affected earlier, individual agents in those newly affected age groups tend to have later first observed exposure step indices.

A layer with elevated post-trough attributed exposure incidence increases the probability that an individual active in that layer experiences a new exposure transition after the city-wide infectious trough.
Greater susceptible depletion at the trough leaves fewer susceptible person-steps in each age band, reducing the post-trough rebound ratio of band exposure hazard relative to its trough value.

Higher entropy means exposure activity is spread across more contact layers; this dilution reduces the likelihood that any single layer sustains consecutive active exposure steps, shortening its active run.

When exposures are more evenly distributed across layers (higher entropy), the probability that a given new exposure is attributed to any particular layer falls, because no layer dominates the exposure mix.
